title: Cells: the tiny living rooms that make up every living thing

summary.text: This unit is about cells. A cell is the smallest piece of a living thing that is itself alive. Every living thing is built from cells: you, a mango tree, an ant and a mushroom. Most cells are far too small to see with your eyes alone, so you will make and use magnifiers to see them in onion skin and in the inside of your own cheek. Some living things are just one cell, and even one cell can sense the world, make choices and remember a little. Scientists agree that all life is made of cells. They still do not know how the very first cell began.
summary.art: A child holding a thin onion skin up to a phone camera with a water drop on the lens, and a zoomed-in bubble showing rows of brick-shaped cells.

intro.hook: Look at the back of your hand. It looks like one smooth thing. What if it were really made of millions of tiny living pieces, each one alive by itself?
intro.text: About 360 years ago, an English scientist called Robert Hooke cut a thin slice of cork, the bark used for bottle stoppers. He looked at it through a microscope, a tool that makes tiny things look big. He saw rows of little empty boxes, like a honeycomb. He called them cells, from a Latin word for a small room. Today you will look for these little rooms in an onion from your kitchen. Then you will look for them inside yourself.
intro.art: A drawing of a man in a long coat and wig peering into an old brass microscope, with a slice of cork beside him and a circle showing honeycomb-like boxes.

outcomes: I can say what a cell is: the smallest living piece of a living thing.
I can explain that all living things are made of one or more cells, and that new cells come only from cells.
I can make a simple magnifier and use it, or a microscope, to look at onion skin and cheek cells, and draw what I see.
I can compare onion cells and cheek cells, and say how they look alike and how they look different.
I can sort things into: made of living cells now, made of cells that were once alive, and never made of cells.
I can describe how small cells are, using a size ladder where each step is 10 times smaller.
I can give examples of single cells that sense, choose and remember, and say what scientists still argue about.

terms.meaning: The smallest piece of a living thing that is itself alive. It is a tiny bag of watery living stuff with a thin skin around it.
terms.example: The thin skin inside an onion is one layer of cells, side by side like bricks in a wall.
terms.art: A single brick-shaped onion cell, drawn big, next to a real onion.

terms.meaning: Something that is alive. It takes in food, grows, makes more of its own kind and responds to the world. Every living thing is made of cells.
terms.example: A neem tree, a cat, a mushroom and you are all living things.
terms.art: A neem tree, a cat, a mushroom and a child standing in a row.

terms.meaning: A tool with lenses that makes tiny things look much bigger, so we can see them.
terms.example: A doctor's lab uses a microscope to look at drops of blood.
terms.art: A simple school microscope with a glass slide on its small stage.

terms.meaning: Any lens that makes things look bigger. A magnifying glass, a drop of water, or a phone camera zoomed in can all magnify.
terms.example: A drop of water on a clear plastic sheet makes the newspaper letters under it look bigger.
terms.art: A drop of water on a plastic sheet making a newspaper letter look huge.

terms.meaning: A clear, curved piece of glass, plastic or water. It bends light so things look bigger or smaller.
terms.example: Spectacles have lenses. So does your eye.
terms.art: A pair of spectacles and a glass marble, with light lines bending through them.

terms.meaning: The very thin skin around every cell. It holds the cell's watery inside in, and lets some things pass in and out.
terms.example: It works a little like the thin skin on a soap bubble, which holds the air inside.
terms.art: A soap bubble next to a round cell, both with a thin shiny skin.

terms.meaning: A stiff box that plant cells have outside their membrane. It gives them their straight edges and helps plants stand up.
terms.example: Onion cells look like bricks because of their walls. Your cheek cells have no walls, so they are soft and floppy.
terms.art: An onion cell drawn as a box with thick walls, next to a soft, round cheek cell.

terms.meaning: A dark round spot inside many cells. It holds the instructions the cell uses to live and grow.
terms.example: When you colour onion skin with a drop of iodine or food colour, a darker dot often shows in each cell. That dot is the nucleus.
terms.art: An onion cell with a small dark dot inside it, circled.

terms.meaning: A living thing that is just one cell. That one cell does everything: it eats, moves, senses and makes more of itself.
terms.example: The bacteria that turn milk into curd are single-celled living things.
terms.art: A bowl of curd with a zoomed-in circle full of tiny rod-shaped bacteria.

terms.meaning: A living thing made of many cells that work together, each doing its own job.
terms.example: You, a banyan tree and an ant are many-celled living things.
terms.art: A child made up of many tiny coloured tiles, like a mosaic.

terms.meaning: Tiny single-celled living things. They are found almost everywhere: in soil, water, curd and inside you.
terms.example: Bacteria in your gut help you break down food.
terms.art: A drop of water with many tiny rods and dots moving in it.

terms.meaning: A tiny single-celled fungus. It eats sugar and gives out a gas that makes dough and idli batter rise.
terms.example: The bubbles in dosa and idli batter come partly from yeast and bacteria.
terms.art: A steel vessel of rising idli batter, with bubbles, and a circle showing round yeast cells.

terms.meaning: The big idea that all living things are made of cells, and that every new cell comes from a cell that was already there.
terms.example: A seed grows into a tree by its cells making more cells. No cell ever forms out of dust.
terms.art: One cell splitting into two, and a tiny seedling beside it.

terms.meaning: A dye that colours parts of a cell, so they are easier to see.
terms.example: A drop of iodine or blue ink on onion skin makes the cell walls and the nucleus show up.
terms.art: A dropper putting one drop of coloured liquid on a thin onion skin on a glass slide.

terms.meaning: To notice something about the world, like light, heat, a touch or a smell.
terms.example: A bacterium senses sugar in the water around it, much as you smell food cooking.
terms.art: A tiny bacterium turning towards a cloud of sugar dots.

terms.meaning: A nerve cell. Neurons are long, thin cells that pass signals to each other. Your brain is made of about 86 billion of them.
terms.example: When you touch something hot, neurons carry the message from your finger to your brain in a split second.
terms.art: A tree-like neuron cell with long branches, sending a spark down its tail.

terms.meaning: A tiny length. Ten millimetres make one centimetre. On a ruler, it is the gap between the smallest lines.
terms.example: A grain of rava, or semolina, is about one millimetre across.
terms.art: A ruler, zoomed in, with one small grain of rava sitting between two millimetre lines.

explanations.definition: A cell is the smallest piece of a living thing that is itself alive. It is a tiny bag of watery living stuff, with a thin skin around it.
explanations.description: Think of a brick wall. The wall is big, but it is built from many small bricks. A living thing is built in the same way, from cells. But a cell is not a dead brick. Each cell is alive by itself. It takes in food, uses it, gets rid of waste, and can make a new cell. The thin skin around every cell is called the membrane. It keeps the cell's inside in, and lets some things in and out. Most cells are so small that many could fit on the full stop at the end of this sentence.
examples: The thin skin inside an onion layer is one sheet of cells, like a wall of bricks.
The inside of your cheek is lined with soft, flat cells that keep coming off and being replaced.
A single grain of yeast powder holds many yeast cells, each one alive.
explanations.art: A brick wall turning into a sheet of onion cells, each brick becoming a living cell with a dot inside.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what a cell is.

explanations.concept: All living things are made of cells
explanations.definition: Every living thing is made of one cell or many cells.
explanations.description: In 1838 a German plant scientist, Matthias Schleiden, said that every plant is made of cells. A year later his friend Theodor Schwann said the same about animals. Since then, scientists have looked at millions of living things. Every single one is made of cells: trees, worms, mushrooms, fish and people. Some are just one cell. Others, like you, are made of trillions. A grown-up's body has about 30 trillion cells. A trillion is a thousand times a thousand times a million. Things that were never alive, like stones, glass and plastic, have no cells at all.
examples: A mango leaf, a moth's wing and the skin of your finger are all made of cells.
A stone or a steel spoon has no cells, because it was never alive.
A wooden table is made of the walls of cells that were once alive in a tree.
explanations.art: A big circle with a tree, an ant, a mushroom, a fish and a child, each with a small zoomed-in window showing its cells.
explanations.context: This card explains the biggest idea about cells: every living thing is made of them.

explanations.concept: New cells come only from cells
explanations.definition: Every new cell is made when a cell that already exists splits into two.
explanations.description: Long ago, many people thought living things could appear out of mud, or meat could make maggots by itself. Careful tests showed this is not true. In the 1850s, a scientist called Robert Remak watched cells and showed that new cells come from old cells splitting in two. Rudolf Virchow made the idea famous in 1855, with the Latin words 'omnis cellula e cellula'. It means every cell comes from a cell. Remak was not given the credit he deserved for many years. Part of the reason was that he was Jewish, and universities in his country held Jewish scientists back. So every cell in you came from a cell, which came from a cell, all the way back to the first cell on Earth.
examples: You began as one single cell. It split into two, then four, then many, and became you.
A cut on your knee heals because the skin cells around it split and fill the gap.
Curd sets because a few bacteria cells keep splitting until there are billions.
explanations.art: One cell splitting into two, then four, then eight, like a chain of paper dolls, with a baby at the end of the chain.
explanations.context: This card explains where new cells come from.

explanations.definition: Most cells are between a tenth of a millimetre and a thousandth of a millimetre across. That is too small to see with our eyes alone.
explanations.description: Your eyes can just about see a speck as small as a tenth of a millimetre, like a fine grain of dust. Many plant cells are about that size, so a strong magnifier can show them. Your cheek cells are smaller, about half a tenth of a millimetre. Bacteria are much smaller still. About a thousand of them could sit in a line across one millimetre. To see cells, we need a lens. A lens bends light so that the tiny thing fills more of our eye. A few cells are huge. A single cotton fibre is one long cell. Some nerve cells in your body run all the way from your back to your toes.
examples: A grain of rava is about one millimetre across. About ten onion cells fit side by side across it.
A cotton fibre from a cotton boll is one single long cell.
The yolk of a new bird's egg starts as one single cell.
explanations.art: A size ladder: a child, a hand, an ant, a grain of rava, an onion cell, a cheek cell and a bacterium, each ten times smaller than the last.
explanations.context: This card is about how tiny cells are, and why we need lenses to see them.

explanations.concept: How a magnifier shows us cells
explanations.definition: A magnifier is a curved, clear lens that bends light so a small thing looks bigger.
explanations.description: Light travels in straight lines until it passes into something clear, like glass or water. Then it bends. A lens is curved, so it bends the light from a tiny thing outwards. When that light reaches your eye, the tiny thing looks bigger. A round drop of water is a lens too. That is why a dewdrop on a leaf makes the leaf's lines look bigger. A microscope has two or more lenses, one after the other. Each one makes the picture bigger again. A school microscope can make things look 100 or even 400 times bigger.
examples: A drop of water on clear plastic makes newspaper letters under it look bigger.
A magnifying glass makes the lines on your fingertip look like ploughed fields.
A phone camera with a water drop on its lens can take photos of onion cells.
explanations.art: Light lines passing through a curved drop of water and spreading out, so a tiny letter under it looks big to an eye.
explanations.context: This card explains how lenses and magnifiers let us see things as tiny as cells.

explanations.concept: Onion cells: a wall of living bricks
explanations.definition: The thin skin inside an onion layer is one sheet of plant cells, each with a stiff wall around it.
explanations.description: When you peel the see-through skin from inside an onion layer, you are holding a sheet that is only one cell thick. That is why light passes through it, and why you can see the cells. Onion cells are long boxes, fitted together like bricks. Their straight edges come from the cell wall, a stiff box that plant cells have around their membrane. Walls help plants stand up without bones. If you add a drop of iodine or ink, a darker round dot often shows inside each cell. That is the nucleus, the part that holds the cell's instructions.
examples: Onion cells look like long bricks in rows.
A stained onion cell often shows a dark dot, its nucleus.
Leaf peel from a plant like Rhoeo, with purple undersides, shows coloured cells in the same brick-like pattern.
explanations.art: A thin onion skin peeled from an onion layer with tweezers, and a circle showing long brick-shaped cells, each with a dark dot.
explanations.context: Remember the onion skin you looked at? This card explains what you saw.

explanations.concept: Cheek cells: the soft cells that line your mouth
explanations.definition: The inside of your cheek is lined with flat, soft animal cells with no walls.
explanations.description: If you gently scrape the inside of your cheek with a clean flat stick, you collect thousands of cells. Under a microscope they look like flat, rough-edged pancakes or fried eggs, often folded. They have no cell wall, so they are floppy and roundish, not boxy. Each one has a nucleus, a darker dot near the middle. Your mouth sheds these cells all the time, and new ones grow from below to replace them. So you leave a few of your own cells on every cup you drink from.
examples: Cheek cells look like flat fried eggs, with a dark dot as the yolk.
Animal cells, like cheek cells, have no wall. Plant cells, like onion cells, do.
Your skin cells are flat like cheek cells. The outer ones are dead and keep flaking off.
explanations.art: Several flat, fried-egg-shaped cheek cells, some folded, with dark dots in their middles, coloured light blue.
explanations.context: Remember scraping the inside of your cheek? This card explains the cells you saw.

explanations.concept: One cell can be a whole living thing
explanations.definition: Many living things are just one cell. That single cell eats, moves, senses and makes more of itself.
explanations.description: In 1674 a cloth-seller in Delft, a town in the Netherlands, looked at a drop of lake water through a tiny lens he had made himself. His name was Antonie van Leeuwenhoek. He saw little creatures swimming, turning and bumping into each other. He called them 'animalcules', little animals. Nobody had ever seen them before. Many were single cells. Later he even found bacteria in the white gunk scraped from his own teeth. Today we know that single-celled living things are the most common life on Earth. They live in soil, seas, hot springs, ice and inside us.
examples: The bacteria that set milk into curd are single cells.
An amoeba in a pond is one cell that changes shape as it creeps along.
The green slime on an old water tank is made of millions of tiny single-celled algae.
explanations.art: A drop of pond water drawn big, full of different single cells: a trumpet shape, a slipper shape, a blob and tiny rods.
explanations.context: This card is about living things that are only one cell.

explanations.definition: In a many-celled living thing, cells stay together and share the work. Different cells do different jobs.
explanations.description: You began as one cell, smaller than a grain of sand. It split again and again. As the cells multiplied, they became different kinds. Some became skin cells, some blood cells, some bone cells and some nerve cells. Your body has about 200 kinds of cells. They all came from that first one. A tree works the same way. Its root cells drink water. Its leaf cells make food from sunlight. No single cell in you could live long in the wild on its own. Together, they make you.
examples: Red blood cells carry oxygen. Nerve cells carry messages.
In a leaf, some cells make food from sunlight, and others form tiny doors that let air in.
Cells in the root tip of a seedling keep splitting, so the root grows down.
explanations.art: A child drawn as a city made of many kinds of cells: red blood cells as delivery vans, nerve cells as telephone wires, skin cells as walls.
explanations.context: This card explains how many cells live together as one body.

explanations.concept: Brains are made of cells too
explanations.definition: A brain is a crowd of cells called neurons, which pass signals to each other.
explanations.description: When you think, remember or feel, cells in your brain are sending signals. A neuron is a long cell with branches. Tiny charged bits called ions flow in and out through its skin. This sends a signal along the cell, like a spark running down a fuse. At the end, the neuron releases chemicals that tell the next neurons what to do. Your brain has about 86 billion neurons. That number was counted carefully in 2009 by a team led by a Brazilian scientist, Suzana Herculano-Houzel. So a thought is many cells sensing and signalling together.
examples: When you touch a hot tawa, nerve cells carry the message to your spine and you pull your hand back fast.
Learning to ride a cycle makes some links between your neurons stronger.
An ant's tiny brain has about a quarter of a million neurons.
explanations.art: A brain drawn as a forest of tree-like neurons, with sparks passing from branch to branch.
explanations.context: This card is about the cells that make up your brain.

explanations.description: A single cell has no brain and no nerves. Yet scientists have watched single cells sense, choose and remember. A bacterium called E. coli swims towards sugar. It does this by remembering, for a few seconds, how much sugar it smelled before. If there is more now, it keeps swimming. If there is less, it tumbles and tries a new direction. A trumpet-shaped single cell called Stentor, about one millimetre long, was poked with tiny specks in an experiment. It tried one way to escape, then another, and then swam away. A yellow slime mould, which is one giant cell, found the shortest path through a maze. Scientists agree on what these cells do. They argue about whether to call it thinking.
examples: E. coli bacteria swim towards food by comparing now with a few seconds ago.
Stentor tried bending away, then closing up, then swimming off when specks kept landing on it.
A slime mould in Japan joined oat flakes in a pattern much like Tokyo's railway map.

perspectives.who: Many cell scientists, such as those who study slime moulds and bacteria
perspectives.explanation: Sensing, choosing and remembering are the basic parts of thinking. Single cells do all three. So thinking began long before brains, and brains built on what cells could already do.
What a bacterium does is clever chemistry, not thinking. Real thinking needs many neurons linked in a brain. Calling it 'thinking' stretches the word too far.
The question depends on what we mean by 'thinking'. If it means 'using what you sense to choose well', cells think. If it means 'having an inner feeling of thinking', nobody knows if cells have that.

explanations.art: A small trumpet-shaped Stentor cell bending away from a cloud of specks, with thought-bubble arrows showing its next tries.
explanations.context: This card asks whether one cell, with no brain at all, can think. Scientists argue about this.

explanations.concept: Wood, cotton and cork: cells that were once alive
explanations.definition: Many things in our homes are made of cells that have died, leaving their walls behind.
explanations.description: When Robert Hooke looked at cork in 1665, the little rooms he saw were empty. The cork came from the bark of a cork oak tree, and its cells had died. Only their walls were left. Wood is the same. It is made of the strong walls of dead tree cells. Cotton is the long single cells of a cotton plant's seed hairs. Paper is made from crushed plant cell walls. So a wooden spoon is not alive, but it was made by living cells. A steel spoon was never made of cells at all.
examples: A cork bottle stopper is made of empty cell walls.
A cotton kurta is woven from millions of single plant cells.
A newspaper is made of the crushed walls of plant cells.
explanations.art: A wooden spoon, a cotton thread and a cork, each with a zoomed-in circle showing empty cell walls.
explanations.context: This card is about things that were made by living cells, but are not alive now.

explanations.concept: Where the first cell came from
explanations.description: All cells come from cells. So where did the very first cell come from? Nobody knows for sure. Fossils of tiny cells show that life began on Earth at least 3.5 billion years ago. One idea is that oily bubbles formed in warm water, the way oil makes round drops in dal. Some bubbles may have trapped simple molecules that could copy themselves. Over a very long time, such bubbles might have become the first living cells. Scientists are testing these ideas in labs. Nobody has yet made a living cell from non-living stuff.
examples: Oil dropped into water forms round bubbles with a skin, a little like a cell's membrane.
The oldest fossils of cell colonies are layered rocks called stromatolites.
Every living thing today seems to come from one shared ancestor cell.
explanations.art: A warm ancient sea with round oily bubbles floating in it, a few with tiny chains inside them.
explanations.context: This card is about the open question of how the first cell began. Scientists only have ideas.

agreed.text: All living things are made of one or more cells.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have looked at millions of living things with microscopes. Every plant, animal, fungus and bacterium is made of cells.

agreed.text: Every new cell comes from a cell that was already there.
agreed.evidence: Under the microscope, scientists can watch a cell split into two. Nobody has ever seen a cell form from non-living stuff.

agreed.text: A cell is the smallest thing that is alive by itself.
agreed.evidence: A single cell can take in food, grow and split. The parts inside a cell cannot live on their own if the cell is broken open.

agreed.text: Plant cells have a stiff wall. Animal cells do not.
agreed.evidence: Onion cells look like boxes with straight edges. Cheek cells are soft and floppy. Stains show the plant walls clearly.

agreed.text: Single cells can sense their world and change what they do.
agreed.evidence: Bacteria swim towards food and away from harm. Scientists have tracked them under microscopes since the 1970s.

challenging.claim: Living things can appear by themselves out of mud, meat or rotting food.
challenging.who: Many thinkers for over 2,000 years, including Aristotle. This idea is called spontaneous generation.
challenging.for: Maggots seem to appear on old meat. Tiny creatures seem to appear in water left standing.
challenging.against: In 1668 Francesco Redi covered some jars of meat with cloth. No maggots appeared, because flies could not lay eggs. In the 1860s Louis Pasteur showed boiled broth stayed free of microbes if nothing could fall in. New life comes only from life.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of where living things come from, and why scientists gave it up.

challenging.claim: Only brains can think. A single cell just follows simple chemistry.
challenging.for: Brains do things no cell can, like talking and doing sums. A bacterium's choices can be explained by its chemicals.
challenging.against: Our brain cells also work by chemistry and charged bits flowing. Single cells sense, choose and remember. Slime moulds solved mazes and learned to ignore harmless bitter tastes.
challenging.context: This card is about whether thinking needs a brain. Scientists argue about it.

challenging.claim: You have ten times more bacteria cells in you than your own cells.
challenging.who: A rough guess made in the 1970s and repeated in many books.
challenging.for: There really are huge numbers of bacteria in your gut.
challenging.against: In 2016, Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo counted more carefully. They found about as many bacteria cells as human cells, roughly one to one.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous number that turned out to be wrong.

challenging.claim: Leeuwenhoek was just a shopkeeper who got lucky.
challenging.who: Some scientists in his time, who doubted a man with no university degree.
challenging.for: He had no training in science, and he kept his lens-making method secret.
challenging.against: He made hundreds of lenses, tested again and again, and wrote careful letters for 50 years. When the Royal Society in London doubted him, he sent signed letters from respected people in Delft who had seen the creatures too. Then the Society saw them for itself in 1677.
challenging.context: This card is about a cloth-seller who first saw single cells alive, and why people doubted him.

challenging.claim: Plants can sense and respond, almost like animals, using electrical signals.
challenging.who: Jagadish Chandra Bose, an Indian scientist, about 120 years ago, and some plant scientists today.
challenging.for: Bose measured electrical signals in plants that looked like signals in animal muscles. Today we know plant cells do send electrical and chemical signals.
challenging.against: Plants have no nerves or brain. Many scientists say calling plants 'clever' or 'feeling' goes beyond the evidence.
challenging.context: This card is about whether plant cells sense and respond like animal cells do.

big_questions.q: If you are made of trillions of living cells, is each cell a little 'you'? Or is 'you' something all of them make together?
big_questions.hint: Can one of your cheek cells feel happy? Can you, without your cells?

big_questions.q: You began as one single cell. Where were 'you' before that?
big_questions.hint: That first cell came from your mother's and father's cells. And theirs came from cells too.

big_questions.q: Why are cells so small? Why not one giant cell the size of an elephant?
big_questions.hint: Think of food getting into a cell through its skin. Would it reach the middle of a huge cell quickly?

big_questions.q: A bacterium has no brain, but it swims towards food. Is that choosing?
big_questions.hint: When you walk towards the smell of food, what are you doing?

big_questions.q: Every cell comes from a cell. So how did the first cell begin?
big_questions.hint: Think of oil making round drops in water. Could a bubble be a start?

big_questions.q: A wooden chair is made of cells that were once alive. Is it more like a stone, or more like a tree?
big_questions.hint: What can a tree do that a chair cannot? What do a chair and a tree share?

big_questions.q: Leeuwenhoek was a cloth-seller with no degree, and people doubted him. What makes us believe someone?
big_questions.hint: What did he do to show others he was right?

big_questions.q: If cells in a slime mould can remember, where is a memory kept when there is no brain?
big_questions.hint: The slime mould leaves a trail behind it. Could the trail be a kind of memory?

big_questions.q: All living things are made of cells. Does that make a mango tree, an ant and you a family?
big_questions.hint: Scientists think all cells come from one first cell, long ago.

story.title: The Trumpet in the Tank Water
story.note: The Foldscope paper microscope is real, and Stentor is a real single cell about a millimetre long. Scientists have watched Stentor bend away, reverse its hairs, shrink and swim off when specks land on it (Jennings 1902, Dexter and others 2019), though not every Stentor does these in the same order. Kavya, Rohan, the school and the temple tank are made up.
text: The microscope came in a brown envelope, flat as a chapati. Kavya's teacher had handed one to every child in Class 3, and said only this: 'Look at everything. Then look again.'

Kavya's cousin Rohan was staying with them for the summer holidays. He was twelve, and he knew things. He watched her press out the paper pieces along their dotted lines. 'A paper microscope,' he said. 'Next they'll give you a paper aeroplane and call it a rocket.'

Kavya did not answer. She folded the stiff blue card, tab into slot, the way the picture showed. She pushed the tiny glass bead of a lens into its hole. When she held it up to the window, it was hardly bigger than her palm.

That evening her mother was chopping onions for sambar. Kavya begged one thin, wet layer. From the inside of it she peeled a skin so fine she could see her fingers through it. She laid it on a glass slide, added a drop of water, and slid it in. Then she put her eye almost against the bead and turned towards the tube light.
At first, everything was a grey blur. She moved the slide a little. Then the blur snapped into shape, and she forgot to breathe.

The onion was a wall. Long, pale bricks lay fitted side by side, row after row, each one outlined in a thin, bright line. In some bricks there was a small dark pebble. She moved the slide and the wall went on and on, as if the onion had been built by tiny masons.
'Rohan, the onion is made of bricks!'
'Cells,' said Rohan, not looking up from his phone. 'Everybody knows that. Everything alive is made of cells. You are too.'

Kavya took a clean ice-cream stick and gently scraped the inside of her cheek. She smeared the clear wetness on a fresh slide and touched it with a drop of blue ink. Under the lens floated flat, blue, crumpled shapes, like fried eggs that someone had stepped on. Each had a dark yolk. They were hers. They had been inside her mouth a minute ago.
'These are me?'
'Some of you,' said Rohan. 'Don't get excited. Cells are just bricks. Bricks don't do anything.'

That night Kavya lay awake and looked at the back of her hand in the dark. She thought of the fried eggs, millions upon millions of them, all holding on to each other. Were they just bricks? They did not feel like bricks.

Early next morning, her mother walked with her to the temple tank. The steps were cool and green at the edges. Kavya dipped an empty jam jar and lifted out water, a few threads of green weed, and a little brown cloud of mud. At home she put one drop on a slide and looked.

The drop was a city. Clear slipper-shaped creatures zoomed past, spinning as they went. A grey blob crept along, pushing out a soft arm and then flowing into it. Tiny green beads rolled by. And on a thread of weed, holding on with a narrow foot, stood a pale blue-green trumpet.

Its wide mouth was fringed with hairs, beating so fast they blurred into a shimmer. Specks of mud swirled into the trumpet, like leaves into a whirlpool. Kavya looked at the sheet her teacher had given her. There it was, drawn in pencil. 'Stentor. One single cell. Almost big enough to see with your eyes.'
One cell. No brain, no eyes, no hands. Just one cell, standing on a weed and eating.
Rohan came to look, because Kavya would not stop squeaking. He watched for a whole minute. 'It's like a pump,' he said. 'It just sucks things in. A machine.'
Kavya remembered her teacher's other words, written at the bottom of the sheet. 'If you want to know what something can do, ask it a question. Then wait.'

How do you ask a cell a question? Kavya thought about it. Then she took a single straw from the broom, dipped its tip in a pinch of powdered chalk, and held it over the slide. She tapped it once. Fine white specks drifted down into the drop, right over the trumpet.
The trumpet bent away. It leaned, slowly, to one side, like a person ducking from rain.
The specks kept falling. Kavya tapped again.
Now the shimmer of hairs stopped. Then it started again, but the other way round. Instead of pulling specks in, the trumpet was pushing them out, blowing them away from its mouth.
'Did you see that?' whispered Kavya.
Rohan had put down his phone.
She tapped a third time. The trumpet gave up blowing. All at once it squeezed itself down into a tight little ball on the weed, the way Kavya curled up under her quilt when thunder came.
They waited. The ball slowly opened into a trumpet again. Kavya tapped one last time.

This time the trumpet did something new. It let go of the weed. Its narrow foot came free, and the whole cell turned and swam off, out of the chalky cloud and into clear water, until it was gone from the circle of light.
For a long moment neither of them said anything.

'It tried one thing,' said Kavya slowly. 'It bent. That didn't work, so it tried something else. It blew. Then it hid. Then it left.' She looked up. 'That's what I do when I can't open a jar. I try one way, then another way, then I call Amma.'
'But it hasn't got a brain,' said Rohan. He did not say it like a know-it-all this time. He said it like a question.

Kavya thought of the pale bricks of the onion, and the blue fried eggs from her cheek. 'Your brain is made of cells, isn't it?' she said. 'Who taught them how to choose? Maybe they learned it from cells like this one. A long, long time ago.'

Rohan held out his hand for the paper microscope. Kavya gave it to him. He put his eye to the bead and stayed there a long time, looking for the trumpet in the clear water, as if it might come back to tell him more.
story.epiphany: A single cell, with no brain at all, sensed the specks, tried one thing, then another, and chose to leave. Brains are made of cells, so thinking may be older than brains.
ask: What did the onion skin look like to Kavya? What were the bricks really?
Rohan said cells are just bricks that don't do anything. What did the trumpet cell do that changed his mind?
How did Kavya 'ask the cell a question'? Can you think of another way to ask it?
Kavya said she tries one way, then another, when a jar won't open. When have you done that?
Why do you think Rohan stopped sounding like a know-it-all at the end?
